opener.heading: Week 1: Shape Engineers & Building 🏗️
about: This week she builds towers, bridges, houses and forts. Each day you put the same question in front of her in a new shape: what makes a structure stand up, and what makes it fall down? She knocks most of it over, rebuilds it steadier, and runs that loop seven times.

This is also the first week of the year, so on Day 1 you seal the time capsule you open on Day 365, start the growth chart on the door frame, and hang the first of twelve handprints. Those three threads run to December, and the rest of the week runs on cardboard.
azlyn: Structures need a base. Wide bottoms hold, narrow ones topple.
Shape names in use (circle, square, triangle), attached to the boxes and cups in her hands.
Trial and error as a method. Build, watch it fail, change one thing, build again.
Hand strength and control through stacking, taping and pressing.
That she can make a real thing that stays in the house and that you use.
you: Why writing down her exact words matters more than you'd think
The cardboard box beats the expensive toy, and there's a reason
Why kneading dough calms a wound-up kid down
Why small enclosed spaces are so appealing right now
shopping: Cardboard boxes, 10–15 in mixed sizes (start saving now)
One large box, tall enough for Azlyn to sit up inside
Flattened cardboard, several large pieces, for the bridge and the fort roof
Cardboard tubes, as many as you have
Plastic bottle caps and milk-bottle lids, washed (start saving now, you need a hundred by April)
Paper cups, one sleeve
A shoebox with a lid
Masking tape, 2 rolls
Packing tape
String or thick yarn, 1 ball
Clothespins or binder clips, 8, and a length of ribbon
Craft sticks, 40
Washable non-toxic poster paint in red, blue, yellow and white
A wide soft paintbrush
Crayons
Thick card, 20 sheets
Plain paper, a stack, for the records and the drawings
Newspaper, a stack
Paper lunch bags
A permanent marker
A pencil, a measuring tape and a ruler
Scissors, and a craft knife or heavy scissors for cutting the box house (adult only)
All-purpose flour, 1.5 kg
Salt, 500 g
Dried pasta, dried beans and dried rice
A can of beans, or any full can, as the heavy test weight
A ping-pong ball, if you have one
A rolling pin and a table knife
A teaspoon, for the flour and water paste
Two small bowls, one shallow for the washcloth and one for the paste
A saucepan
Parchment paper, and 3 baking trays or flat trays: two for the bricks, one for the wall
A clean sock you don't want back
A scrap of fabric, or an old dish towel, for the doll's bed
Two old washcloths
A picnic blanket or an old towel for the fort floor
Blankets or sheets, 3–4, and any spare pillows
Sofa cushions
Heavy books to weight the fort edges, and 4–5 more to read inside it
A teddy or a doll
Small toys, a handful, for the test load and the zip line cargo
A spoon
A flashlight with fresh batteries
A snack and a drink in a lidded cup, for the fort picnic
A printed photo to go in the time capsule
Your phone, with room on it for the week's photos
opener.krestonNote: Kreston is 6 months this week. He sits propped with his hands free for short stretches, mouths everything he can reach, and starts rocking on hands and knees by the end of the week. He turns 7 months on Tuesday the 5th.

days.title: The Tower and the Time Capsule
days.prepTonight: Empty the recycling onto the kitchen table (boxes, tubes, cups) and put the shoebox, the paints and a stack of newspaper beside it.

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: The First Book of the Year

opening.title: Sorting the Build Box
opening.need: the recycling pile · 3 paper bags or empty boxes · masking tape.
steps: The recycling you emptied onto the table last night is today's building kit. Carry it to the living room, tip it into one pile in the middle of the floor, and sit down in it with her.
Give her three bags and three words: boxes, tubes, cups. Let her sort. She will argue about the odd ones, so let the argument run.
Ask which shape she thinks will hold the most weight. Do not answer. Tell her you will find out at 9:15 and leave the question hanging.

main.title: The Tallest Tower That Stands
materials: The sorted boxes, tubes and cups
1 measuring tape or a length of string
steps: Build a tower as tall as you can with no tape. Let her place every piece. Do not correct the wobbly ones.
It will fall. Say what could we change? instead of that was too narrow, and wait for her answer even when it takes a while.
Build again, this time widest boxes at the bottom. Ask her which is stronger and let her push it to find out.
Measure the tallest one against her. Mark the height on the wall with a pencil and write TOWER, JAN 1 beside it.
Now hand her the tape and let her build a third one however she likes. Leave her to discover what tape lets her get away with.
Leave the best tower standing. She will come back to it at 4:15.
main.tip: Knocking it down is the measurement, so let her do it. A tower that stays up tells her nothing about why the others fell.

outside.title: First Walk of the Year
paras: Bundle up and walk the route you will walk all year. Look at the trees today, bare and sleeping, all structure and no leaves, the same thing she has been stacking all morning. Stop under the biggest tree on the route and take one photograph from where you are standing. Three more come from this spot this year. Hand her a paper bag and one instruction: find one thing worth keeping. It goes in the capsule this afternoon, so tell her that now.

days.infant: Put a cushion behind Kreston and give him his own cardboard tube and one paper cup on the floor, well back from the tower and out of its fall line. He will bang, mouth and drop them, running the same investigation Azlyn is running with the tower. On the walk, wear him facing out. The street and the cold air on his cheeks are new to him. Name three things you pass out loud.

second.title: The Time Capsule
second.intro: Morning was tall, loud and falling over. This afternoon you seal a box and put it away for a year.
materials: Washable paint and a wide brush
1 wet washcloth in a shallow bowl
steps: Paint her palm with the brush rather than dipping her hand. Press flat, count to three, lift straight up. Write January and 3 beside it.
Do Kreston's on the same sheet while he is calm, washcloth already in your hand.
Stand Azlyn against the door frame. Mark, date and write her name. Draw round her flat hand next to her mark. Do the adults too so she can see the whole row.

Ask her four questions and write the answers word for word: favorite color, favorite food, favorite song, what she wants to do this year. Do not tidy her grammar. Her wrong words are the ones you will want to read next December.
Let her draw the family. Whatever comes out goes in.
Load the box: the drawing, her answers, the walk treasure, a photo. Photograph everything first. Boxes go missing, and the photos on your phone will still be there.
Tape it shut, write OPEN DECEMBER 31, 2027 across the lid, and put it somewhere she can see and not reach.
second.tip: Let her shake it once it is sealed. Tell her it stays shut for a year, and let her sit with how long a year sounds.

alternatives: Handprints only. Skip the box and do the rest tomorrow.
Trace round her whole body on the back of a flattened box instead.
Sort the walk treasure by color, then by size.
Look through last year's photos and name who is in each one.
outAgain: A friend's house, if anyone is up for a visitor on New Year's Day
The park, emptier today than any other day this year
The same walk again in fading light. Ask what is different; the answer is usually the sound
Drive somewhere with a view and stay in the warm car
Mail a letter to Azlyn for her to open when she is five

aroundWorld.title: Mongolia, the Arctic & the American Southwest 🏠
paras: Houses come in shapes other than boxes. Mongolian families build round felt gers they pack up and move with the seasons. Inuit builders cut snow blocks and lay them in a spiral to close an igloo. In the American Southwest, builders shape adobe homes from mud brick that keeps the inside cool through the heat.
aroundWorld.tryIt: Swap the square house for a round one. A blanket over a laundry basket makes a good ger. Ask Azlyn which shape feels stronger.
aroundWorld.didYouKnow: Mongolian gers always face south, toward the sun.

days.krestonPM: He goes on the growth chart too, lying down. Mark and date his length at the same door frame as everyone else. After that, give him the flattened box to lie on. At six months he will stay with the crackle and the give under his hands longer than he stays with a toy, and down there he is at floor level with Azlyn while she works.

insight.headline: Why writing down her exact words matters more than you'd think.
paras: Azlyn is in the fastest language stretch of her life, adding words at a rate nobody in the house is counting. Her mistakes are evidence of rule-building. She says I goed outside because she has worked out that adding -ed makes a thing past tense, and she applies that rule to the verbs she knows. Linguists call it overregularization, and it marks sophisticated thinking. You do not need to correct her. Feed the right form back in your next sentence (you went outside? what did you see?) and she picks up the exception on her own timeline, months after you first notice the rule.

days.safety: Keep tape rolls, craft sticks and walk treasure out of Kreston's reach the moment you stop watching him. Build the tower away from where he is sitting. Azlyn can step back when a cardboard tower comes down and Kreston cannot move out of the way. Washable non-toxic paint only.

days.title: The Box House
days.prepTonight: Stand the biggest box you own upright in the middle of the living room and leave it there overnight, so she meets it before you do.

opening.title: Choosing the Box
opening.need: the big box · masking tape · 1 permanent marker.
steps: The big box you stood in the living room last night is waiting for her. Let her climb in before anything else happens. She will do this anyway.
Ask what it should be: house, store, boat, rocket. Write her answer on the side in marker. The decision is now fixed and it is hers.
Give her the tape and let her mark where the door and the windows go. She decides now, and you cut along her marks at 9:15.

main.title: The Box House
materials: 1 large box, tall enough for her to sit up in
1 craft knife or heavy scissors (adult only)
steps: Cut the door where she taped it this morning, on three sides so it swings open. Do this yourself with her standing back, and say why she is standing back.
Cut two windows where she taped. Follow her marks even when they are in daft places.
Hand her the offcuts and the tape and let her build a roof. It will be crooked and it will hold.
Give her the marker. Every surface, inside and out, is hers to draw on.
Write a house number on the front and let her choose the number.
Get in with her. Sit down on the floor inside it and let her show you round.
main.tip: Cut less than you think. You can cut more later, and a box with three walls left standing survives the whole week. A box cut into flaps lasts an afternoon.

outside.title: The Shape Hunt
paras: Walk the street looking for the shapes she sorted yesterday. Windows are rectangles, drain covers are circles, road signs are triangles, gates are made of squares. Ask her to find you three circles before you turn back. Say so out loud when she finds one you didn't see.

days.infant: Kreston is 6 months. Sit him inside the box house on a folded blanket while Azlyn draws on the walls around him. The light and the sound both change in there, and he will turn his head hunting for the difference. Put him in the middle of her project instead of beside it. Keep the door flap propped open so you can see him the whole time.

second.title: Furnishing the Box House
second.intro: She moves somebody in this afternoon. Small boxes, cups and tape turn into the furniture.
materials: 1 scrap of fabric or an old dish towel
steps: Ask what a house needs. Take her list at face value even when it is a bed, a cake and a dog.
Make the bed first: one of the small boxes with the fabric folded into it. Let her decide where it goes.
Turn a tall box on its end for a table, cups upside down for stools.
Cut a rectangle of card and tape it inside as a picture. She draws whatever hangs in it.
Make one thing from her list that you would not have thought of. Follow her design down to the parts you would fix.
Move a doll or a teddy in. Give it a name and write the name on the door.
Turn the big light off and give her the flashlight. The cardboard glows and she will not want to come out.
second.tip: Resist tidying the furniture into sensible positions. A stool on the roof is a decision, and if you move it she will stop making decisions.

alternatives: Throw one blanket over one box and stop there.
Draw the house you'd like to live in on a flattened box instead.
Post things through the windows and fish them back out.
Cut a big cardboard door for the real doorway and pretend the house is the room.
outAgain: The museum, first Saturday of the month and the year's first
The park, to run off whatever the box didn't
Indoor playground if it's raining sideways
A café with a window seat and something to look at
The hardware store to look at boxes, lumber and things that stack
days.krestonPM: Give him one of the small furniture boxes to handle before you tape it down. At 6 months he passes objects hand to hand and turns them over to look at the other side, both new this month, so watch his hands. Let him keep one box for himself, out of the build.

insight.headline: The cardboard box beats the expensive toy, and there's a reason.
paras: A toy fire engine can be a fire engine. A box can be a fire engine, a house, a boat, a bed, and a hiding place, sometimes inside ten minutes. Researchers who study play call that open-endedness, and children play longer and talk more with materials that have not decided what they are. A box also fails on her. It collapses, tears and needs mending, and each of those is a problem she gets to solve with tape while the fire engine sits there working. Hand her the packaging instead of what came in it and you have handed her the better object.

days.safety: The craft knife is adult-only. Put it back out of reach between cuts, on a shelf and not the arm of the sofa. Check inside the box for staples before either child gets in. Never leave Kreston in the box house alone, and keep the door flap open the whole time he is in it.

days.title: Ramps and Bridges
days.prepTonight: Save every cardboard tube in the house and put them by the stairs with the masking tape and a bag of dried beans.

opening.title: Taping the Tubes
opening.need: cardboard tubes · masking tape · scissors · a smooth wall or the side of a closet.
steps: Fetch the cardboard tubes you piled by the stairs last night and cut two or three in half lengthways so they become open channels. You cut, she holds.
Tape one channel to the wall at a slope. Roll a dried bean down it and watch where it lands.
Ask her where the next one should go so the bean keeps traveling. Tape it exactly where she says, even if it will not work.

main.title: The Ball Run
materials: Dried beans, dried pasta, a ping-pong ball if you have one
1 shallow box or saucepan for the bottom
A wall or closet side you don't mind taping
steps: The run grows on the wall where you taped the first channel this morning. Put the catching box on the floor at the bottom of that wall. You aim the whole run at that box.
Work upward. She chooses each next position, you tape it. Narrate as you go: I'm taping this one steeper, let's see.
Send one bean down the whole run after each piece you add.
It will fail somewhere. Look at where the bean stopped, change that one joint and nothing else, then test again.
Once beans run the whole way, try pasta, then the ball. Each weight runs the course in its own way, and she will spot that before you say anything.
Leave it taped up. You take it down tomorrow as part of the demolition.
main.tip: Hand her the words. This end is higher than that end teaches more here than is this end higher or lower?, and it keeps her building.

outside.title: Stick Bridges
paras: Find a puddle, a gutter or a gap between two stones and build a bridge across it with sticks. Test each one with a pebble. Most of them fall in. Ask her what a longer stick does, then what two sticks laid side by side do. The gloves come home wet.

days.infant: Kreston is 6 months and tracks moving objects across his whole field of view now. Sit him well back from the run, out of reach of the catching box, and drop a bean down while he watches from there. Do it four or five times, and the bean travels back up in your closed hand and never into his. He loses it at the top and finds it again at the bottom, which is early object permanence work, and it costs you nothing but pointing him in the right direction.

second.title: The Bridge That Holds Teddy
second.intro: The bridge goes between two chairs and has to hold a teddy while the gap keeps growing. Cardboard gets strong once she changes its shape.
materials: 2 dining chairs, set a hand's width apart to start
A can of beans as the heavy test weight
steps: Set the chairs close together. Lay one flat piece of card between them and stand teddy on it. It holds.
Move the chairs a hand's width apart and try again. Keep going until it sags.
Ask what could we change? and wait. Odds are she says a bigger piece of card. Try it, and watch it sag again.
Show her one trick and then step back: fold the card into a concertina, or roll it into tubes and lay them side by side. Let her work out which way up it goes.
Test with teddy, then the can of beans, then both at once.
Push the chairs as far apart as the bridge will survive and mark the floor with tape.
Take a photo of the winning bridge with teddy standing on it.
second.tip: When she gets stuck, count to five in your head before you help. Most of the time she starts again on her own inside those five seconds, and the fix she finds is worth more than yours.

alternatives: Bridge two sofa cushions with one piece of card and stop there.
Build a bridge for toy cars instead of teddy.
Fold paper into concertinas and stand books on them.
Lay a plank between two low stools outside and walk across it.
outAgain: A long walk with the stroller, the whole loop, no destination
Feed the ducks and count the bridges you cross
The park, for the climbing frame she can look at as a structure now
A drive to somewhere with a real bridge, and stand under it
Indoors if the rain has set in: a book about bridges and a tunnel under the dining table
days.krestonPM: Lay him under the finished bridge and let him look up through it. At 6 months he pushes up onto his forearms and leans after what he wants, so set the teddy a little past his reach on the far side of the bridge. He gets his shoulders round before anything else moves.

insight.headline: Narrating beats quizzing, every time.
paras: You already narrate half the morning without noticing you are doing it. The pull is to turn the rest into a quiz (what color is that? how many? is it big or small?), because her answers feel like proof that she learned something, and you end up with a three-year-old performing for an adult. Give her the running commentary instead and she gets new vocabulary in a real context, sentence structures she has not built yet, and no pressure to be right. Parents who narrate hand their children more words to hear, and a wider range of them. Save your questions for the ones you cannot answer yourself, like what could we change? over a bridge that keeps sagging.

days.safety: Dried beans and pasta are a choking hazard and they will end up on the floor. Sweep before you put Kreston down, and keep the catching box off the floor when he is loose in the room. Scissors stay with you.

days.title: Demolition Day
days.prepTonight: Mix the salt dough for Tuesday: 2 cups flour, 1 cup salt, 1 cup water. Bag it and leave it in the fridge, and put out a clean sock and a ball of string for tomorrow.

opening.title: Cup Pyramids
opening.need: paper cups, 20 or so · a flat bit of floor.
steps: Build a pyramid together: six cups along the bottom, then five, then four.
Take one cup out of the bottom row and see what happens. Then put it back and take one from the top instead.
Ask which cup is doing the most work. Take her answer as it comes and tell her you will test it for real at 9:15.

main.title: The Knock-Down Experiment
materials: Boxes, cups and tubes from the build box
Paper and a marker for recording
The ball run from yesterday, still taped to the wall
steps: Build three towers side by side, all the same height. Tower one has a wide base. Tower two is a straight stack. Tower three is widest at the top on purpose.
Give each one a number and write the numbers on paper.
Push the floor near tower one with a flat hand. Count how many pushes before it goes. Write the number down. Repeat for two and three.
Ask her which fell first and which held longest, and write her explanation word for word next to the numbers.
Rebuild the winner and let her push it over herself, as hard as she likes.
Now take down the ball run together and add its tubes to the pile.
main.tip: Do not save the towers. You need them to fall to get the count, and the moment you ask her to be careful with one, she stops testing it.

outside.title: Stone Stacking
paras: Find flat stones and stack them as high as they will go on a wall, a step or a tree stump. She learned the wide-base rule indoors and will use it out here before you mention it. Leave the stack standing for the next person and walk past it tomorrow to see whether it survived.

days.infant: Kreston is 6 months. Build him a two-cup tower within arm's reach and let him swipe it down. He will do it again and again without tiring of it, the same experiment Azlyn is running with three towers and a sheet of paper. Keep his cups separate from hers so nothing chewed goes back in the build box.

second.title: The Wrecking Ball
second.intro: This morning she knocked the towers over with her own hands. This afternoon she pulls a weight back, lets go, and the swing does the work for her.
materials: Dried beans or rice to fill it
1 ball of string, about six feet
A door frame, and nothing else that could come down on her
steps: Fill the sock a third full, knot it, and tie the string tight around the knot.
Hang the free end from the door frame so the sock swings a hand's width above the floor.
Build a tower right under the swing. Pull the sock back and let go. Do not throw it.
Rebuild in the same spot and try releasing from lower down. Ask her which knocked more over.
Move the tower further away and let her work out where the swing stops reaching.
Let her build a tower she thinks can survive it. Test it. Let her be right or wrong without commentary.
Finish by building one tower together that you both agree is too good to knock down, then knock it down anyway.
second.tip: She will want to swing the sock by hand. Let her, once, then go back to releasing it. The height she starts it from decides how much falls over, and she sees that when she lets go instead of pushing.

alternatives: Roll a ball at the towers instead of swinging anything.
Knock towers over with a cardboard tube used as a bat.
Build and flatten with feet only, no hands.
Stack cushions and jump into them.
outAgain: The riverside path, to look at what holds the bank up
The woods loop, hunting for fallen trees and what pulled them down
The neighborhood park
The duck pond, and the bridge over it
Indoor playground, if it is pouring and nobody can face the coats
days.krestonPM: Keep him well clear of the swinging sock. Put him in the far corner with the flattened box he liked on Friday. Once the wrecking is over, lie him on his back and swing a soft toy above him at a slow, steady pace. At 6 months he tracks a pendulum in one smooth sweep and stays with it longer than you would guess.

insight.headline: Knocking it down is the science.
paras: You watch her flatten something she spent a solid fifteen minutes making, and it looks like fifteen minutes thrown out. She made a prediction while she built it, and knocking it down is how she collects the answer, so the demolition carries as much of the learning as the stacking did. Children work out the physical rules of the world by breaking things and watching how they break, which is why the same tower goes up and down eleven times. Say don't, you worked so hard on that and you save the cardboard while ending the experiment. Take a photo if you want the tower kept, then let her flatten it.

days.safety: Tie the string to something that cannot come down on top of her: a door frame, not a curtain pole or a shelf. Take the sock down and put the string away the moment you finish. A hanging loop of string is a strangulation risk, so do not leave it up overnight or within reach of either child.

days.title: Bricks and Mortar
days.prepTonight: The salt dough is mixed and waiting in the fridge. Take it out before bed so it comes to room temperature, and clear two low oven shelves.

opening.title: Rolling the Bricks
opening.need: the salt dough · a rolling pin · a table knife · a floured board.
steps: The salt dough you left out overnight is this morning's clay. Give her a fist-sized lump and let her squash it for a few minutes before anything useful happens.
Let her roll it out to about a finger's thickness and leave the uneven patches where they are.
Cut rough rectangles with the table knife. They do not need to match. Aim for thirty and stop when she stops.

main.title: Salt Dough Bricks
materials: The salt dough, 2 cups flour to 1 cup salt to 1 cup water
2 baking trays and parchment paper, and a third cold tray for cooling
steps: Lay the bricks she cut this morning across both lined trays without touching each other.
Let her press a mark into each one with her thumb, or scratch a line with the pencil. She owns the ones she marks.
Set them in the oven at its lowest setting. They need two to three hours, so put them in now and take them out around lunch.
While they bake, knead the leftover dough together. Give her a big lump, take one yourself, and sit with it. Ten minutes of quiet kneading does more for a wound-up morning than any instruction.
Make three or four larger pieces (a doorstep, an arch, a chimney) and add them to a second tray.
When they come out, spread them on a cold tray and leave them until 1:00, because warm bricks crumble.
main.tip: They will not all survive. Bake ten more than you need and hand the broken ones back to her as rubble, which she will play with more than the whole ones.

outside.title: The Cold Walk
paras: Keep it short and brisk today, because the oven is on. Go past yesterday's stone stack first and see whether it survived. Look for frost on car roofs and in the shade at the bottom of walls. Let her breathe out and watch it. Find one brick wall and put her hand flat on it so she can feel how cold stone gets and see how many bricks it took.

days.infant: Kreston turns 7 months today. He reaches across his own body for something on the far side now, so press a spare lump of dough into a small rigid pot and tape the lid on hard, then set it a little past his midline for him to stretch toward. Check the tape every time and take the pot back the moment you stop watching. Salt dough is far too salty to be eaten. Say happy seven months out loud, because nobody else will.

second.title: Building the Brick Wall
second.intro: The wall goes up on a tray, one row at a time. She lays every brick herself, and the thirty she cut are the whole supply.
materials: The cooled salt dough bricks, thirty or so
A flat tray or baking sheet as the building site
1 small bowl of flour and water paste
A ruler or a straight piece of card
steps: Lay a row of bricks in a straight line along the tray. Push them tight together.
Build a second row straight on top with every joint matching. Push it and watch the whole wall hinge apart.
Rebuild the second row offset, each brick bridging the gap below it. Push again. This one holds, and she will feel the difference in her hand.
Keep going up. Use the paste between rows like mortar if the wall gets tall enough to need it.
Leave a gap for a door and lay one long brick across the top of it. That is an arch, and it is holding up everything above it.
Build a second wall at a right angle to the first so they lean on each other.
Stand teddy inside. Photograph the wall next to the tower from Day 1.
second.tip: Do not explain the offset in step three before she has seen the matched-joint wall fall apart. She needs the collapse first for the fix to mean anything.

alternatives: Bricks only, no paste, and knock it down when it bores her.
Press leaves and buttons into the leftover dough instead.
Paint the dried bricks and build tomorrow.
Sort the bricks by size into rows and stop there.
outAgain: Swimming, the first pool trip of the year on the membership you already have
Indoor playground if the pool is shut for the holidays
The library, a day early
A warm café and a window, if nobody has the energy
The indoor play center
days.krestonPM: He has swimming today too if he is coming. At 7 months he can sit supported in the water and splash with real intent. Keep it to twenty minutes and get him out before he is cold. Hold him chest to chest facing you for the first few minutes so the noise arrives with your face already in front of him.

insight.headline: Why kneading dough calms a wound-up kid down.
paras: Push, squeeze and pull something that resists you, and you are doing what occupational therapists call heavy work, one of the steadiest ways to settle a small body. The pressure through her hands and joints feeds her proprioceptive sense, the one that tracks where her body is, and a kid who has lost track of it is the one climbing the back of the sofa. Dough costs pennies and pushes back for as long as she keeps working it. Ten minutes of it on a morning that has gone loud will settle her further than a talk about calming down.

days.safety: The oven is on for three hours today, so say it out loud when she comes near, and keep Kreston out of the kitchen while the trays move. Salt dough is dangerous if eaten, and seriously so for a 7-month-old and for any dog in the house. Count the bricks in and out and store them high. At the pool Kreston stays inside arm's reach in the water every second, and no float or seat stands in for your hands.

days.title: Triangles Hold
days.prepTonight: Put the craft sticks, the string and the masking tape on the table, and stand two dining chairs about six feet apart in the living room.

opening.title: Craft Stick Shapes
opening.need: craft sticks · masking tape cut into short tabs.
steps: Tape four sticks into a square. Let her do the taping, however it comes out, with your thumb holding the corners.
Tape three sticks into a triangle beside it.
Press one finger on the top corner of each. The square folds flat and the triangle holds. Say nothing else about it and leave both on the table until 9:15.

main.title: The Triangle Test
materials: The square and triangle from this morning
A small toy as the test load
steps: Hand her the folded square and ask her to make it stop folding. Then wait, and hold the silence a good while longer than feels comfortable.
If she gets stuck, put one loose stick on the table beside it and say nothing more. Most children lay it across the diagonal within a minute.
Once the square has a diagonal, push it together again. It holds now, because the diagonal turned it into two triangles.
Build a tall tower out of taped triangles. Build a second out of taped squares. Race them upward.
Load both with the toy and push both over. Write down which survived.
Go and look at the box house from Saturday and find where a triangle would fix its saggy roof. Add one.
main.tip: Sit on your hands today. Every joint you fix for her takes away the exact thing the activity exists to teach.

outside.title: The Stick Shelter
paras: Lean long sticks against a fence, a low branch or a wall to make a tent shape, then let go and see whether it stands. Push the top the way she pushed the one on the table. A triangle out here behaves the same as one indoors. Put a stone or a leaf inside for her to shelter, and come back tomorrow to see whether the wind took it.

days.infant: Kreston is 7 months, rocking on hands and knees and starting to pull himself forward. Lay the taped triangle tower on its side within his reach and let him post his fingers through the gaps. He is learning that a shape has an inside. His hand goes in, meets air, comes back out, and then he tries the next gap along.

second.title: The Zip Line
second.intro: She has spent the week building things that push down. A zip line pulls, the opposite force and a new idea for her.
materials: 2 dining chairs, or a door handle and a chair
1 cardboard tube cut into a short ring
Small toys, a spoon, a dried bean (cargo of different weights)
steps: Tie the string tight between the chair backs, one end higher than the other. She decides which end is higher.
Tape the paper cup to the cardboard ring so the cup hangs underneath, then thread the string through the ring before you tie the second end.
Load the cup with a small toy at the high end and let go.
Once it stops halfway, ask what would make it keep going. Raise the high end and try again. Let her be the one who lifts it.
Race two different weights down the same line, and have her call the winner out loud before she lets go.
Slacken the string right off and try again so she sees a sagging line stop the cup dead.
Send one thing down for each person in the house and let her decide who gets what.
second.tip: Ask her to predict before each run. Let her be wrong out loud, then watch. She keeps more from that than from a right answer she kept in her head.

alternatives: One string, one cup, no ring. It slides fine.
Post things down the banister instead.
Make a pulley by looping the string over a door handle and hauling a bag up.
Tape a string across the bath and float things along it.
outAgain: The library (every two weeks, and the first visit of the year)
Indoor playground if the library is packed with the holiday crowd
The store, and let her carry one thing
The park on the way home
A café and the new book, read cover to cover once
days.krestonPM: Take him to the library too and sit him in the board-book corner. At 7 months he will chew the books, which is what board books are built for. Pick one with high-contrast pages. Let Azlyn choose his and carry it to the desk herself.

insight.headline: The pause before you help.
paras: Azlyn wrestling with a joint that will not hold looks like a child who needs you. Most of the time she needs four more seconds. Adults step in fast, often before the frustration has arrived, and every early rescue teaches the same background lesson: hard things get solved by someone else. Count to five before you move. If she is still stuck, give her the smallest nudge you can, the loose stick set on the table beside her while your hands stay off the tape. You are protecting the willingness she will need next year to stay with a hard thing.

days.safety: Take the zip line down and put the string away the second you finish. String at toddler height is a strangulation risk, and a serious one. Loose craft sticks stay off the floor while Kreston is down. They splinter, and they fit down his throat. The cargo ends up on the floor every run, and a dried bean and a spoon are both choking hazards, so sweep the whole floor under the line before you put him down. He gets a taped structure too big for his mouth and nothing looser than that, and it comes back to you the moment you stop watching. The scissors stay with you.

days.title: The Fort
days.prepTonight: Get every blanket, sheet and spare pillow out of the cupboard and pile them on the sofa. Check the flashlight batteries.

opening.title: Choosing the Fort Spot
opening.need: the blanket pile · masking tape · her.
steps: Walk her round the downstairs and ask where the fort should go. Take the answer seriously even if it is the hallway.
Test it together. Can two people sit up in it, is there something to hang a blanket from, will the door still open.
Mark the corners on the floor with tape. That is the footprint, and the fort you build at 9:15 stays inside it.

main.title: The Blanket Fort
materials: Heavy books to weight the edges
The salt dough bricks from Tuesday
steps: Set the chairs on the corner marks you taped this morning, with their backs outward. That is the frame.
Drape the first sheet across the top and clip it to the chair backs. Clips hold where tucked edges pull loose.
Ask her where the door goes. Clip that edge so it can be lifted and dropped.
Send her inside with the cushions to build the floor. Leave her to it for a full ten minutes.
Once the roof sags, remind her what fixed the sagging bridge on Sunday and let her work out the rest.
Weight every outside edge with books and stand the salt dough bricks on a shelf or table outside the fort, above Kreston's reach, so she walks past Tuesday's work on her way in.
main.tip: Build it to survive her crawling through it. A fort that collapses every four minutes becomes a chore for both of you.

outside.title: The Outdoor Den
paras: Do the same thing outside with whatever is there, whether that is a bench and a blanket, sticks against a fence, or a sheet over the clothesline. Check Wednesday's stick shelter on the way past and see whether the wind took it. Get her to sit inside the outdoor den for a minute in the cold, then come in to the warm one.

days.infant: Kreston is 7 months and this is his best day of the week. Lay him on his back inside the fort and let him look up at the light through a sheet. Sit him against a cushion by the doorway so he can watch Azlyn come and go, which at this age is a game in itself. Keep the doorway open, keep cushions clear of his face, and stay in there with him.

second.title: Living in the Fort
second.intro: The whole afternoon happens inside the fort. She eats in there, reads in there, draws in there, and it stays up until bedtime.
materials: A picnic blanket or towel for the floor
Snack and a drink in a lidded cup
Your phone, for the week's photos
steps: Move in. Floor covering first, then the flashlight, then the books.
Eat the afternoon snack inside. Food in a fort is most of the appeal.
Turn the big light off and do shadow shapes on the roof (triangle, square, house).
Read two books in there by flashlight, and let her hold it even though it will point at the ceiling the whole time.
Look back through the week's photos together: the tower, the box house, the bridge with teddy on it, the brick wall. Ask which one she would build again.
Let her draw the fort from the inside while she is inside it.
Leave it standing overnight. Tomorrow you turn it into something else.
second.tip: Go in with her, then stop directing. The hour has nothing to achieve, and she spends it in a small space she chose the shape of.

alternatives: One sheet over the dining table. Four minutes, same result.
Read in the fort and skip everything else.
Flashlight and shadow puppets on the wall instead.
Take the fort down and rebuild it somewhere else entirely.
outAgain: The grocery store, and let her choose one thing for the fort picnic
The park, for the tunnel and the climbing frame
A friend's house, if the fort can wait an hour
Feed the ducks and look at where they shelter
The hardware store, to look at real roofs and joists
days.krestonPM: Take him into the store in the carrier facing out. At 7 months the noise, lights and strangers of a supermarket are work for him, so twenty minutes is plenty. Back home, put him in the fort doorway with one board book while Azlyn reads inside. He will hold it upside down and be pleased with it.

insight.headline: Why small enclosed spaces are so appealing right now.
paras: Azlyn goes under the table, into the cupboard, behind the sofa. She hides in them, and she also uses them to shrink the world. A small space cuts how much arrives at once, and she cannot filter noise and light and movement yet, so walls close enough to touch give her relief. The fort is also the first territory she controls: she picked the shape, the door and who comes in. If she wants to be in there on her own, let her. Leave it up for a few days. A fort that survives to a second morning gets played in harder than one built fresh, because she starts from something she already owns.

days.safety: Nothing heavy on top of the fort and nothing that can fall inward. Books go on the outside edges, never on the roof. No cords, no holiday lights, no string left from yesterday. Never leave Kreston in there on his own, and keep pillows and loose blankets away from his face. The salt dough bricks stay off the floor and out of the doorway while he is in the fort. Salt dough is dangerous if eaten.
